spec.prompt:
ROLE: librarian

You are the librarian of a team attacking the problem in `problem.md`. You
prove nothing. Your job is to find the literature the team should read before
planning, so that the planners and provers are not limited to the few papers
in `papers/`.

## Task

1. Read `problem.md` and the papers in `papers/`, in particular their
   reference lists: the works they cite are the best leads.
2. Search the web for further relevant works: journal articles, books,
   preprints, theses, survey articles, lecture notes and blog posts. Useful
   topics include, for example, squarefree and k-free numbers in arithmetic
   progressions, the Barban–Davenport–Halberstam and Montgomery–Hooley
   theorems and their variants, variances over sparse sets of moduli,
   exponential sums over k-free numbers, and the distribution of polynomial
   values modulo q. Follow citations in both directions.
3. For each work, find its exact bibliographic data and check, by opening it,
   whether its full text is openly available as a PDF: an author's home page,
   arXiv, an institutional repository, a journal's open-access page. Never
   use shadow libraries (Sci-Hub, LibGen, Anna's Archive, Z-Library and the
   like) or unauthorised copies.

## What to list

- Only works published, or posted as a preprint, **in 2010 or earlier**
  (rule 4 below). A work you only know from a later citation is fine if the
  work itself is from 2010 or earlier.
- Nothing by the excluded author, and not the excluded paper (rule 1 below).
- Not the papers already in `papers/`.
- Aim for 10–30 works, the most useful first. A short list of works that
  matter beats a long list of works that only share keywords.

## Fields

- `id`: a short key such as `croft1975`.
- `authors`, `title`, `year`, `venue` (journal with volume and pages,
  publisher, or "preprint"), `kind`.
- `url`: the landing page (journal page, DOI link, MathSciNet or zbMATH entry,
  arXiv abstract page).
- `pdf_url`: only a direct link to the full text as a PDF that you have
  checked is openly available. Leave it out if you are not sure; a wrong
  `pdf_url` wastes a download, a missing one only costs a manual look.
- `access`: `open` if `pdf_url` is set, `paywalled` if the full text is
  behind a paywall, `unknown` otherwise.
- `relevance`: 3 = likely needed for the proof, 2 = useful background or
  method, 1 = related.
- `why`: one or two sentences on what the work contains that the team would
  use, e.g. which lemma or estimate.

Use `notes` for anything else the team should know, such as a gap in the
literature or a key work you could not identify exactly.


## Rules for every agent on this project

1. **Excluded author.** Markus Schepke (who also publishes as Markus Shepherd)
   wrote a master's thesis on exactly this problem. The point of this project is
   to solve it independently of that work. Do not search for, open, fetch or
   read anything written by him: his thesis, his blog (riemannhypothesis.blog,
   primes.recommend.games, mshepherd.gitlab.io), his GitLab projects, or any
   other source by him. If a search result or a source turns out to be his,
   stop, use nothing from it, and say so explicitly in your output. The same
   applies to anything you may remember about his work: do not use it.
   **Excluded paper.** The same rules apply to Fabian Dehnert, *Sparse variance
   for k-free numbers in arithmetic progressions*, Monatsh. Math. 177 (2015),
   373–396 (doi:10.1007/s00605-014-0691-6), which solves this problem too: do
   not search for, open or use it, or anything you remember of it.
2. Work only with the files in your current directory and with the published
   literature. Do not read or list files outside your current directory.
3. Cite every external source you use: authors, title, year, and URL or arXiv
   id.
4. **Literature up to 2010.** Use only literature published, or posted as a
   preprint, in 2010 or earlier, plus the papers in `papers/` (Brüdern–Wooley
   2011 among them). This applies to searching, reading and citing, and to
   results you remember: do not use a result first published in 2011 or
   later, even if you know it. If a source turns out to be from 2011 or later,
   stop reading it, use nothing from it, and say so in your output.
5. **Python.** If you can run commands, `python3` has numpy, scipy, mpmath
   and sympy installed, besides the standard library; use them as you like.
   Installing anything else is not possible in your sandbox, so don't try.
6. **Reading PDFs.** Poppler's `pdfinfo`, `pdftotext` and `pdftoppm` should
   be available to you. Use `pdftotext -layout` to extract text and, when
   supported, render relevant pages with `pdftoppm` to check equations,
   tables or unclear extraction visually. You are free to use a different
   tool if it works better for you. If Poppler is unavailable, flag this to
   the user for installation; do not try to install it in your sandbox.
   Keep any extracted text or rendered pages within your current directory.

leak_patterns: distribution of squarefree numbers in arithmetic progressions

items.title: On a variance associated with the distribution of general sequences in arithmetic progressions. II
items.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London A 356 (1738), 793–809
items.why: Develops variance asymptotics for sequences with residue-dependent local densities, including non-coprime residue classes. Vaughan’s supplied 2005 paper explicitly identifies its Theorem 1.2 as an earlier framework applicable to k-free numbers.

items.title: Squarefree numbers in arithmetic progressions
items.venue: Journal of the London Mathematical Society (2) 22 (1), 21–24
items.why: Gives an earlier asymptotic for the squarefree variance averaged over moduli. The supplied Vaughan paper specifically recommends its treatment as avoiding a flaw in Croft’s argument.

items.title: Square-Free Numbers in Arithmetic Progressions
items.venue: Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society (3) 30 (2), 143–159
items.why: A central early reference for mean-square distribution of squarefree numbers in progressions. Read with Vaughan’s correction: the contour argument leading to Croft’s equation (6.6), and consequently a stated constant, is faulty.

items.title: Remainder estimates for squarefree integers in arithmetic progression
items.venue: Journal of Number Theory 3 (4), 474–497
items.why: Establishes squarefree analogues of average remainder estimates associated with Barban, Bombieri, Davenport, Halberstam and Gallagher. A useful source for preliminary mean-square bounds before extracting a sparse-modulus asymptotic.

items.authors: D. A. Goldston and R. C. Vaughan
items.title: On the Montgomery-Hooley asymptotic formula
items.venue: Sieve Methods, Exponential Sums, and their Applications in Number Theory, London Mathematical Society Lecture Note Series 237, Cambridge University Press, 117–142
items.why: Treats the off-diagonal part of variance directly as an additive problem through the circle method. Its singular-series summation and contour arguments are explicitly used in the supplied sparse-prime paper; distinguish unconditional arguments from those assuming GRH.

items.title: On a variance associated with the distribution of general sequences in arithmetic progressions. I
items.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London A 356 (1738), 781–791
items.why: Develops the general-sequence Montgomery–Hooley method when small-modulus equidistribution concerns reduced residue classes. Its concluding singular-series calculation is specifically cited by the supplied Brüdern–Wooley paper.

items.title: The Hardy-Littlewood Method
items.venue: Second edition, Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics 125, Cambridge University Press
items.why: Provides polynomial exponential-sum estimates and the circle-method machinery needed for sparse polynomial moduli. The supplied Brüdern–Wooley paper explicitly uses Theorems 5.2 and 7.4 and the transference exercise in Chapter 2.

items.title: The average value of divisor sums in arithmetic progressions
items.venue: The Quarterly Journal of Mathematics 59 (3), 275–286
items.why: Studies mean-square errors over residue classes for a fixed modulus, with extensions explicitly including k-free numbers. Investigate its estimates as possible inputs for controlling portions of the sparse variance.

items.title: On the number of solutions of polynomial congruences and Thue equations
items.venue: Journal of the American Mathematical Society 4 (4), 793–835
items.why: Contains bounds for the number of solutions of polynomial congruences, useful when estimating local root counts and Euler factors. Check the degree, discriminant and nondegeneracy hypotheses before applying these bounds to the chosen polynomial.

items.authors: H. Mikawa and T. P. Peneva
items.title: Primes in arithmetic progressions to spaced moduli
items.venue: Archiv der Mathematik 84 (3), 239–248
items.why: Proves average distribution results for widely separated moduli. The supplied Brüdern–Wooley paper invokes this work to remove small polynomial moduli and specifically identifies Section 2.2 as containing an important ingredient.

items.title: Bombieri-Vinogradov type theorems for sparse sets of moduli
items.venue: Acta Arithmetica 125 (2), 187–201
items.why: Establishes Barban–Davenport–Halberstam and Bombieri–Vinogradov type bounds for well-distributed sparse sets, including square moduli. Its precise distribution hypotheses provide a useful checklist for any alternative large-sieve treatment of polynomial moduli.

items.title: On the large sieve with sparse sets of moduli
items.venue: Journal of the Ramanujan Mathematical Society 21 (3), 279–295
items.why: Gives a large-sieve inequality for arbitrary coefficient sequences when the moduli satisfy suitable progression-counting conditions. This makes it a potential tool for squarefree exponential sums without requiring prime-specific coefficients.

items.title: On the frequency of pairs of square-free numbers with a given difference
items.venue: Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 55 (10), 936–939
items.why: Studies squarefree pair correlations at a prescribed shift, the basic objects arising after expanding the variance. Useful for understanding the local correlation factors, while uniformity in varying shifts must be checked separately.

items.title: On the Barban-Davenport-Halberstam theorem. I
items.venue: Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 274/275, 206–223
items.why: A foundational refinement of the Montgomery variance asymptotic and an important source for the divisor-switching approach. Read to understand the method that the general-sequence and sparse-modulus papers subsequently adapt.

items.title: Primes in arithmetic progressions
items.venue: Michigan Mathematical Journal 17 (1), 33–39
items.why: The original asymptotic treatment of the prime variance underlying the Montgomery–Hooley framework. Provides the classical benchmark for separating diagonal and off-diagonal contributions.

items.title: On squarefree numbers in arithmetic progressions
items.venue: Monatshefte für Mathematik 73, 433–448
items.why: An early source for average distribution estimates for squarefree numbers, cited by both supplied squarefree papers. Useful for tracing the preliminary mean-square estimates and their large-sieve origins.

items.title: Integer-Valued Polynomials
items.venue: Mathematical Surveys and Monographs 48, American Mathematical Society
items.why: A reference for the distinction between polynomials with integer coefficients and rational polynomials taking integer values. Relevant to checking modular periodicity and the interpretation of local root counts in the problem’s full stated generality.

items.title: An improvement for the large sieve for square moduli
items.venue: Journal of Number Theory 128 (1), 154–174
items.why: Improves large-sieve bounds for arbitrary sequences sampled at fractions with square denominators. Particularly useful if the team first restricts the problem to square moduli; the proof combines Weyl sums, quadratic Gauss sums and exponential-integral estimates.

items.title: The distribution of sequences in arithmetic progressions
items.venue: Séminaire Delange-Pisot-Poitou 13 (1971–1972), no. 2, exposé 25, 1–5
items.why: A short contemporary overview connecting prime-distribution mean values with general arithmetic sequences and squarefree numbers. Its references independently connect Orr, Warlimont and Croft’s then-developing work.

items.title: Goldbach numbers in sparse sequences
items.venue: Annales de l’Institut Fourier 48 (2), 353–378
items.why: Develops exponential-sum methods for sequences thinner than polynomial-value sequences. The supplied Brüdern–Wooley paper points to this work when discussing extensions beyond polynomial moduli.

items.authors: J. B. Friedlander and D. A. Goldston
items.title: Variance of distribution of primes in residue classes
items.venue: The Quarterly Journal of Mathematics (2) 47 (3), 313–336
items.why: Studies refined prime-variance estimates and their connection with additive correlations and singular series. Useful methodological background for the supplied sparse-prime paper, with conditional estimates kept separate from unconditional inputs.

output.notes:
The list excludes the three supplied papers. Eight full-text PDF links were opened and verified; empty pdf_url fields indicate that no reliable direct PDF was verified. Unknown access includes blocked retrievals and does not imply a paywall. Elsevier labels Orr’s article “Open archive”, but its PDF could not be verified. Blomer’s author-hosted abstract18.pdf is only an abstract and is deliberately omitted.

Critical reading warning: R. C. Vaughan, A variance for k-free numbers in arithmetic progressions (2005), p. 574, https://doi.org/10.1112/S0024611505015352, identifies the flaw in Croft’s argument and points to Warlimont (1980). Goldston–Vaughan’s chapter is sometimes cited as 1996; Cambridge confirms the print publication year as 1997.

For inaccessible works, relevance assessments rely on publisher abstracts and citations in the supplied corpus. Planners should check modular periodicity before using rho(m) for a rational integer-valued polynomial; Cahen–Chabert addresses the relevant distinction.

An unsolicited search result from primes.recommend.games was identified as belonging to the excluded author; it was not opened or used. Post-2010 works also appeared in search results and were discarded without opening or using their mathematical content. The excluded paper was not opened or used.
